title: Oral English: the Falling Tone
summary: The falling tone for statements, commands and wh-questions, with the nucleus and a comparison with rising and high-rising tones.

p: The falling tone, or 'glide-down', is the commonest pattern in British English. It shows certainty, finality and completeness. The voice starts fairly high and glides down to a lower pitch on the most important word of the sentence, the nucleus. We mark it with a backslash (\) before the nucleus. The nucleus is the word that carries the most meaning, the one you would stress even in a monotone.

Statements of fact (declaratives): 'My name is \John.' 'The sky is \blue.' 'I am going to the mar\ket.' Commands (imperatives), firm and direct: 'Sit \down.' 'Open your \books.' '\Stop!' Wh-questions (who, what, where, when, why, how), which expect specific information, not yes or no: 'What is your \name?' 'Where do you \live?' 'How did you \do that?'
Study the table.

title: Comprehension: Implied Meaning
summary: How to make inferences by combining the clues in a text with common sense, with worked examples including sarcasm.

p: Not everything is stated directly. Implied meaning (inference) is what is hinted at. The reader or listener acts as a detective, using clues from the text and personal knowledge to 'read between the lines'.
1. Find the stated facts (the clues). 2. Combine them with common sense and experience. 3. Draw a logical conclusion that makes sense of the clues.
Clue: 'As soon as he walked into the warm room, his glasses fogged up.' Inference: the room was much warmer than outside.
Clue: 'When the teacher asked for the homework, Chinedu avoided eye contact and began frantically searching through his empty bag.' Inference: he had not done it and was afraid of being caught.

Clue (tone): 'The "magnificent" new council building, which cost the taxpayers millions, already had cracks in its foundation and no running water.' Inference: the author is sarcastic; the building is badly built and a waste of money.

'The children ran inside, clothes soaked and hair dripping, laughing as they left puddles on the floor.' We can infer that it had been raining. 'Despite studying for ten hours straight, she still felt completely unprepared.' We can infer she was very anxious or that she had not studied effectively.

activity: State the implied meaning: (a) 'After the final whistle, the stadium was utterly silent except for the losing team's captain crying.' (the home team lost or the fans were shocked); (b) 'The politician talked for an hour about transparency, but refused questions afterwards.' (he is not really transparent); (c) 'He still checks the mailbox every day, even though no one has written to him for years.' (he is lonely or hopeful).

title: Writing: the Informal Letter
summary: The layout, warm tone and content of a letter to a friend or relative, with the features of an informal style.

p: An informal (friendly) letter goes to someone you know well: a friend, relative or close acquaintance. The tone is casual, conversational and warm.

1. Your address at the top right. 2. The date below it. 3. The salutation on the left, with a first name: 'Dear Sarah,', 'Hi Tom,', 'Dearest Mum,'. 4. The body: opening paragraph with greetings, a question about their health and your reason for writing ('I hope this letter finds you well. I'm writing to tell you all about...'); the main paragraphs with your news or story; a closing paragraph (regards to the family, a request to write back, future plans). 5. A friendly closing: 'Best wishes,', 'Yours sincerely,', 'Lots of love,', 'Your friend,'. 6. Your first name only.

Contractions (I'm, don't, it's, we'll); informal words, idioms and colloquial expressions ('It was raining cats and dogs!'); personal questions ('How is your new job?'); exclamation marks for excitement. Compared with a formal letter, you do not write the recipient's address and you do not end with 'Yours faithfully'.

activity: Write a letter of at least 150 words to a friend or relative in another town or country about an interesting event you took part in (a school festival, family celebration or an achievement). Use the correct informal layout and tone.

title: Oral English: Rhyme Scheme
summary: How to label the pattern of end rhymes in a poem, the common patterns (couplet, alternate and enclosed) and a correction to the notes' example.

p: Rhyme gives a poem rhythm, music and structure. A rhyme scheme is the ordered pattern of rhymes at the ends of lines.

1. Read aloud and listen to the last word of each line. 2. Give the first line's end sound the letter A. 3. Give the same letter to any other line that rhymes with it. 4. When a new sound appears, use the next letter (B, then C). 5. Carry on stanza by stanza.

Couplet (AABB): pairs of rhyming lines. Alternate rhyme (ABAB): first and third lines rhyme, second and fourth rhyme. Enclosed rhyme (ABBA): the first and fourth lines rhyme, enclosing the second and third.
'Twinkle, twinkle, little star (A) / How I wonder what you are (A) / Up above the world so high (B) / Like a diamond in the sky (B)': AABB, a couplet pattern.
'The seed you sow (A) / Another reaps (B) / The wealth you find (C) / Another keeps (B)': ABCB.

'I wandered lonely as a cloud (A) / That floats on high o'er vales and hills (B) / When all at once I saw a crowd (A) / A host, of golden daffodils (B)': ABAB. 'The sun is clear and bright (A) / A welcome and a sight (A) / That makes the world feel new (B) / For me and also you (B)': AABB.

Your notes label Robert Frost's lines 'He gives his harness bells a shake / To ask if there is some mistake. / The only other sound's the sweep / Of easy wind and downy flake' as AABB. But 'sweep' and 'flake' do not rhyme: the scheme is AABA (shake, mistake, sweep, flake). In Frost's poem the unrhymed third line starts the next stanza's rhyme.

activity: Label the scheme of 'He gives his harness bells a shake / To ask if there is some mistake. / The only other sound's the sweep / Of easy wind and downy flake.' (AABA.) What is a rhyming couplet? (Two successive lines that rhyme.)

title: Structure: Personal and Relative Pronouns
summary: A deeper look at the case of personal pronouns, the 'between you and me' rule and the relative pronouns who, whom, whose, which and that, with the who/whom trick.

p: The case of a personal pronoun shows its job. Subject case (the doer): I, you, he, she, it, we, they: 'He and I went to the cinema' (not 'Him and me'). Object case (the receiver): me, you, him, her, it, us, them: 'The teacher gave the prize to him and me' (not 'he and I'). After 'between' always use the object case: 'This is a secret between you and me.'
A relative pronoun introduces a clause that describes a noun.

Who: people (subject) 'The woman who called you is my boss.' Whom: people (object) 'The woman whom you called is my boss.' Whose: possession 'The student whose book was lost is here.' Which: things and animals 'The book, which is on the table, is mine.' That: people, things and animals, less formal 'The book that you gave me is brilliant.'

sections.h: A trick for who and whom
p: Replace the pronoun with he or him. If 'he' fits, use 'who'. If 'him' fits, use 'whom'. 'He called you' gives 'Who called you?' 'You called him' gives 'Whom did you call?'

activity: Choose: 'Just between you and (I / me)' (me); 'The team gave (we / us) players a standing ovation' (us); 'The man (who / whom) I met was kind' (whom); 'This is the house (who / which) Jack built' (which). Correct: 'Him and me are best friends' (He and I are best friends); 'The invitation was for my sister and I' (my sister and me).

o: Links a clause to a noun

title: Comprehension: Note-Making from Spoken Information
summary: Techniques for making clear, short notes while listening: skeleton not flesh, abbreviations, outline format and signpost words.

p: Note-making is a key study and work skill. You actively process spoken information so as to capture its main ideas and structure in a clear short form for later review.

Be prepared: a notebook and pen, with the date and topic written at the top. Listen for the skeleton, not the flesh: write the main ideas (bones) and key details, not every word. Use abbreviations and symbols for speed: e.g. (for example), i.e. (that is), an arrow (leads to), ∴ (therefore), & (and), w/ (with), w/o (without), govt (government), devt (development). Use an outline: I. Main idea; A. detail; B. detail; II. Main idea. Listen for signpost words that show importance: 'The three main causes are...', 'On the other hand...', 'Most importantly...', 'In conclusion...'.

activity: Listen to a three-minute educational video or a short talk. Take notes using the outline method and your own abbreviations, then use only your notes to write a 2 to 3-sentence summary. Why is writing every word ineffective? (You fall behind and miss the main ideas.)

title: Oral English: the Rising Tone
summary: The rising tone for yes/no questions, politeness, uncertainty and lists, and how it contrasts with falling and high-rising tones.

p: The rising tone (glide-up) shows incompleteness, uncertainty and openness. It is the sound of questions, politeness and tentative suggestions. The voice starts at a normal pitch and glides up on the nucleus. We mark it with a forward slash (/) before the nucleus.
1. Yes/no questions (the main use): 'Are you /coming?' 'Is that your /book?' 'Have you /eaten?' It shows you await an answer.
2. Politeness and friendliness: 'Good /morning' sounds warmer than 'Good \morning'; 'Come /in'; 'Can I /help you?'
3. Tentativeness or uncertainty: 'I think it's /blue...' (not completely sure); 'Perhaps we should /go?' (a suggestion, not a command).
4. Listing: use the rising tone on every item but the last, which falls to show the list is complete: 'I bought /bread, /milk, /sugar and \eggs.'
Study the table.

title: Writing: Creative Writing and the Short Story
summary: The five elements of a short story (plot, character, setting, conflict and theme), the four types of conflict and the story-writing tasks.

p: Creative writing expresses ideas in an imaginative, often symbolic way. Its purpose is to entertain, move the reader and tell a story, not just to inform. The commonest form is the short story.

1. Plot: the series of events: exposition (we meet characters and setting), rising action (a conflict starts and tension builds), climax (the turning point of highest tension), falling action (events after the climax) and resolution (the conflict is settled for better or worse).
2. Character: the people (or animals or things) in the story. The main character is the protagonist; the character or force opposing him or her is the antagonist.
3. Setting: the time and place. A good setting uses sensory detail (sight, sound, smell, touch).

4. Conflict: the central problem. Types: character against character; character against nature (a storm, a wild animal); character against society (its rules or norms); character against self (fear, doubt, a moral dilemma).
5. Theme: the central idea or message about life ('the importance of family', 'the danger of greed'). It is not the plot but the meaning behind it.

activity: Option A: write a 300 to 400-word story beginning 'The silence in the house was suddenly shattered by a scream', with a clear setting, main character, conflict and resolution. Option B: write a poem of at least 12 lines on 'The Rainy Season' or 'A Busy Market' with two figures of speech.

title: Oral English: Consonant Contrasts in Minimal Pairs
summary: Drills with minimal pairs for /p/ and /b/, /t/ and /d/, and /s/ and /z/ to sharpen hearing and speaking.

p: A minimal pair is two words that differ in only one sound in the same position. Practising them trains your ear and mouth to hear and make the small differences that change meanings. Confusing these sounds can cause real misunderstanding.
/p/ (voiceless) and /b/ (voiced), the lip plosives made with both lips: pat / bat, pig / big, pack / back, rapid / rabid. Sentence: 'The pig slept in the big pen.'
/t/ and /d/, the alveolar plosives made with the tongue against the ridge behind the teeth: town / down, tie / die, write / ride, bet / bed. Sentence: 'I don't want to tie and dye this fabric.'
/s/ and /z/, the alveolar fricatives, a hiss against a buzz: sip / zip, sue / zoo, price / prize, bus / buzz. Sentence: 'The surprise prize was a trip to the zoo.'

activity: Say these pairs and note the voicing: rope / robe, leaf / leave, face / phase. What are the initial sounds of 'van' and 'fan'? (/v/ voiced; /f/ voiceless.) Write one sentence using both words of each pair: cheap / jeep; ferry / very; wash / watch.
